analysis.one_liner: Lets courts strike down state abortion rules that single out clinics without improving patient safety.
analysis.headline: A bill with 36 Senate backers — all Democrats and one independent — received a single Judiciary Committee hearing in July 2014 and never came to a Senate vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for any government to impose restrictions on abortion that single out the procedure and do not significantly advance women's health or safety — such as rules on clinic buildings, hospital-transfer arrangements, and provider credentials that do not apply to comparable medical procedures, or medically unnecessary extra visits before an abortion. It would also bar states from banning abortion before fetal viability. Patients, providers, or the Attorney General could sue to strike such restrictions, and the bill would override conflicting state laws.
analysis.who_benefits: Women seeking abortion — and the clinics that serve them — especially low-income women, women of color, and women in rural or underserved areas, whom the bill's findings say bear the heaviest burden of state restrictions that make services harder and more expensive to reach.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women seeking abortion, especially low-income and rural women

how_it_helps.text: Bars governments from imposing abortion-specific rules on facilities, staffing, hospital-transfer arrangements, or provider credentials that are not imposed on medically comparable procedures [S3].

Eliminates requirements that a woman make medically unnecessary visits before an abortion, and limits on prescribing medication abortion or providing it by telemedicine that do not apply generally to medicine [S3].
Prohibits bans on abortion before fetal viability and bans after viability that disregard a physician's good-faith judgment about the woman's life or health [S3].
Gives patients, providers, and the Attorney General the right to sue for court orders against unlawful restrictions, with attorney and expert fees paid to winning plaintiffs [S3].

The bill's findings state that existing restrictions fall especially heavily on low-income women, women of color, and women in rural and underserved areas, and also reduce access to contraception and cancer screenings offered by the targeted clinics [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments and localities would lose the power to enforce or enact abortion-specific restrictions, and would face lawsuits and litigation costs when their rules were challenged; states defending a restriction would have to prove by clear and convincing evidence that it significantly advances safety and that no less restrictive alternative exists.

drawbacks.text: The bill would void any conflicting state law, including restrictions already on the books before its passage, effectively transferring abortion regulation from state legislatures to federal courts [S3].

It would prohibit states from banning abortion before fetal viability — a broader rule than the Supreme Court's then-existing standard, which allowed states to restrict abortion after the first trimester so long as the woman's access was preserved [S3].

A state defending a restriction must meet a demanding burden — clear and convincing evidence that the measure significantly advances safety and that no less restrictive alternative exists — which would make it very difficult to sustain rules like hospital-admitting-privilege or clinic-facility requirements that supporters defended as patient-safety measures [S3].

The bill's own text leaves untouched several major access barriers it acknowledges: restrictions on insurance coverage of abortion, parental consent or notification for minors, and clinic violence, which it defers to separate legislation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For women who want the ability to end a pregnancy, the bill would have removed the accumulating patchwork of state rules that make services scarce, delayed, and more expensive, and its findings tie that access to broader clinic services and to low-income and rural women's ability to obtain care at all. The cost is to state-level control: democratically enacted restrictions — including ones their backers describe as health and safety measures — would be struck down under a heavy legal burden, and the bill reaches well beyond codifying the abortion right as the courts had defined it. Whether that is a flaw or the point depends on the reader's view of who should set abortion rules; the bill itself would have settled the question nationally rather than state by state.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in November 2013 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which held one hearing in July 2014 but never voted on it, and the bill never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the Women's Health Protection Act of 2013 on November 13, 2013, joined by 31 original Senate cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced [S5].
The Judiciary Committee held a hearing on the bill on July 15, 2014 (printed as S.Hrg. 113-844), its only committee action [S5].
The bill ended the Congress with 35 cosponsors — 34 Democrats and 1 independent — and no Republican support listed [S4].
No further committee action, floor vote, or chamber vote on the bill appears in the action history through the end of the 113th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments that had enacted abortion restrictions kept them in force, since only a federal law could have struck them down; organizations that support such restrictions also kept the state-level framework they had built since 2010 intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States and groups backing abortion restrictions

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 31 original Senate cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 34 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Senate Republican did.

for.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on July 15, 2014 — the committee's only action on it.

against.name: Patrick Leahy
against.what_they_did: The committee under his chairmanship held a hearing but never took a vote or reported the bill out during the Congress.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; no floor action appears in the record for the entire Congress.

against.name: Anti-abortion advocacy organizations
against.role: National right-to-life groups opposing federal protection of abortion access
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill publicly as an expansion of abortion rights beyond Roe v. Wade; no supporting action by them appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 36 sponsors and cosponsors was a Democrat or independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never received a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would bar states from imposing abortion-specific facility, staffing, credential, and hospital-transfer rules that don't apply to comparable procedures, allowing clinics shut down by such rules to operate and new providers to open [S3]. Clinics' ability to see patients is the same thing women's access depends on.

They would lose the power to enact or enforce abortion restrictions, including pre-viability bans, and would face suits from patients, providers, or the Attorney General [S3]. Their retained interest in restriction is what costs women access under the bill's framing.
The bill would invalidate the state-level restrictions these groups have pushed since 2010 and give providers and patients a new federal cause of action against them [S3].
